Millions of people rely on Medicare to help them save money in retirement while still getting the healthcare they need, and Open Enrollment gives them the annual opportunity to shop for a new plan. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is warning Medicare enrollees that scams are increasingly common, especially during Open Enrollment. If enrollees aren't careful, they might find themselves signing up for a plan that isn't real health insurance, or handing their personal information over to a scammer. Here's what you should know about these Medicare scams, how to spot them, and what you need to do to protect yourself. Read More Here › SPONSORED Medicare search result scams If you perform a search for Medicare plans, Open Enrollment, or a related topic, the top results you receive might not be from genuine government sites. That's because search engines allow individuals to pay for ads that closely resemble official Medicare websites, and those look-alike sites may appear above the real search results. The fake sites feature official-looking logos and keywords, making it difficult to quickly identify them as scam sites. "Bad actors often use web addresses that look similar to government website addresses. They also use keywords and official-looking logos to make you think you're at the real Healthcare.gov or Medicare.gov when you're not," reads the warning. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. What might happen if you click on a scam site According to the FTC, clicking on one of those scam sites could lead to several consequences. It's possible that you might buy a plan that isn't actual health insurance, paying for a service but never actually receiving the coverage you think you're buying. Alternatively, you might be tricked into buying a plan that you hadn't intended to purchase. The sites might also try to capture your personal information and use it for medical identity theft. Medical identity theft occurs when a thief steals your personal information, which might include your name, Social Security number, and Medicare number. Then, the thief uses your information to submit fraudulent claims to Medicare and health insurers. A thief committing medical identity theft might submit claims to have procedures done or to buy medical equipment, leaving you with the resulting bills. Medical identity theft might lead to fake medical records created in your name, and you could potentially face debt collectors. Ultimately, it could impact your credit score. How to spot scam Medicare ads Though these scam Medicare ads appear year-round, the FTC warns that they're much more active around Medicare Open Enrollment, which lasts from October 15 through December 7. It's important to be extra aware of these potential scams during this time. When using a search engine, look for "Ad" or "Sponsored" labels that appear next to search results; these labels identify paid ads. Scroll past those paid ads and look for sites with addresses that end in .gov to confirm they're genuine. To be extra safe, avoid search engines and type trusted site URLs directly into your browser. For example, type Medicare.gov into your browser to go straight to the trusted government site. Medicare phone scams to be aware of Medicare scams aren't just online; scammers may try to contact you by phone, too. For example, some callers might claim that Medicare is issuing updated cards. They might ask you to confirm your medicare number or banking details to receive your updated card. According to the FTC, Medicare cards automatically arrive by mail, and you won't be contacted by phone. Scammers might also call you and offer free genetic testing or equipment. They may ask for your Medicare number, then bill Medicare for the items. If Medicare denies the claim, you might be responsible for the full cost of the testing or item. Benefit cancellation calls are another common scam. A caller might warn you that your Medicare coverage might be suspended unless you immediately verify your Social Security number. According to Medicare.gov, you'll only be required to confirm your personal details if you initiate contact. Bottom line If you suspect you might have been a victim of a scam or that a scammer has contacted you, report the scam to Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227. You may also report the scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, as well as to your state attorney general. Be sure to carefully review your Medicare statements for unfamiliar charges and promptly report anything unusual on your statements. Choosing the best Medicare plan for your needs is an important step in supporting your health and your finances. Just be sure to use extra caution to spot scams and avoid financial mistakes as you shop for a plan during Open Enrollment.
